abstention.statement: GLIPR1 and GABARAPL2 lack any compelling genetic or functional association with restless legs syndrome. Neither gene has variants linked to RLS in the GWAS Catalog, and their model organism knockouts display phenotypes entirely unrelated to sleep or motor function (e.g., increased tumor incidence for Glipr1, and preweaning lethality for Gabarapl2). There is insufficient evidence to integrate them into an RLS disease mechanism.
abstention.what_would_change_this: A well-powered GWAS identifying genome-wide significant associations for GLIPR1 or GABARAPL2 with RLS, or experimental studies showing their direct functional interaction with known risk loci like MEIS1 or BTBD9 in sleep regulatory neural circuits.

falsification.description: Knock out MEIS1 and PTPRD individually in human iPSC-derived neurons and assess for defects in synaptic differentiation and rhythmic activity using multi-electrode arrays. A failure to observe neurodevelopmental or network activity changes would decouple these variants from the proposed synaptic mechanism.

hypotheses.mechanism: MEIS1 and PTPRD are both strongly associated with restless legs syndrome (RLS) via GWAS. MEIS1 is a developmental transcription factor critical for neural patterning, and its loss in mice disrupts circadian sleep/wake cycles. PTPRD is a synaptic receptor tyrosine phosphatase that bidirectionally induces pre- and post-synaptic differentiation, with genetic pleiotropy linking it to neurodevelopmental disorders like ADHD. The convergence of these genes suggests a shared pathophysiological pathway where aberrant synaptic differentiation and altered central nervous system circuitry lead to the sensory-motor symptoms and sleep disturbances characteristic of RLS.
hypotheses.title: Variants in MEIS1 and PTPRD converge on disrupted synaptic differentiation and circadian sleep-wake circuitry.

falsification.description: Perform ubiquitination assays and measure ACO1 protein half-life in human dopaminergic neurons following BTBD9 knockdown. If ACO1 turnover and cellular iron indices remain unchanged, BTBD9 does not regulate ACO1-mediated iron homeostasis.

hypotheses.mechanism: Brain iron deficiency is a central hallmark of RLS pathophysiology. ACO1 acts as a bifunctional iron sensor that regulates the translation of iron homeostasis genes, and its deficiency in mice impairs systemic iron handling. BTBD9, a major genetic risk factor for RLS whose disruption causes abnormal sleep behavior in mice, contains a BTB/BACK domain typical of ubiquitin ligase adaptors and physically interacts with ACO1. We hypothesize that BTBD9 regulates the turnover of ACO1; when BTBD9 is disrupted by RLS-associated variants, aberrant accumulation or dysfunction of ACO1 exacerbates cellular iron deficiency in the central nervous system, thereby precipitating RLS symptoms.
hypotheses.title: BTBD9-mediated turnover of the iron sensor ACO1 is impaired in restless legs syndrome, exacerbating neuronal iron deficiency.
